Patient-reported symptoms:
  Maladaptive Strategies: Rumination: Self-Blame: repeatedly blame myself for what happened, Avoid Driving: Driving or being a passenger in a vehicle, Avoid Conflict: Any situation that might involve disagreement or confrontation
  Threat: Safe Zone Only: I only feel safe in a very limited number of places, Startle to Sounds: I jump or startle at ordinary sounds that would not bother most people, Hypervigilance: Being superalert or watchful or on guard
  Memory: Story Feels Unreal: The memory is so extreme it is hard to believe it actually happened to me, Visual Memories: My memories of the frightening event are mostly pictures or images., Auditory Recall: When I have memories of what happened I sometimes hear things in my head that I heard during the frightening event.

Vignette:
Tien remembered the day the sky over the transit camp cracked open not with thunder, but with synchronized detonations. He was coordinating supply routes for displaced families when the first vehicle approached the perimeter, followed by a second. The air tore apart. In the immediate aftermath, the world folded into sharp, silent frames: a red supply crate overturned against a concrete wall, the glint of twisted rebar, the way the dust hung suspended in the slanted light. The sequence of events felt so violent and absolute that, even now, his mind refused to accept it as a single moment he had survived. When the images surfaced unbidden, they carried the weight of the original moment—the crackle of broken radio transmissions, the low hum of distant generators, the sharp report of gunfire that had echoed through the compound. Those sounds did not fade; they waited beneath the quiet of his present days. As the months passed, the compound’s perimeters disappeared from his awareness, replaced by a rigid geometry of safety. Only a handful of rooms allowed his shoulders to drop: the corner study in his suburban Ohio home, the reinforced briefing room at the regional humanitarian coordination office, the master bedroom. Everywhere else, his nervous system remained tuned to a frequency just below alarm. A dropped stack of files in the supply closet made him flinch as if shrapnel had skipped the linoleum. A car backfiring down the residential street pulled his breath tight against his ribs. He found himself scanning doorways and vehicle mirrors, his gaze never settling, constantly cataloging exits and sightlines as though the ground might again fracture without warning. The incident left him convinced that his own decisions had steered them into the blast radius. In the quiet hours, the same ledger of errors turned over in his mind: which convoy he had approved, which checkpoint he had trusted, the precise minute he had dismissed the initial radio warning. He would sit at his kitchen table for hours, tracing the same mental map, certain that a different call could have kept his team intact. This conviction hardened into practical routines. He stopped allowing himself to ride in cars, citing stiff necks or poor eyesight, when what actually stopped him was the helplessness of being secured behind glass while the road ahead remained unpredictable. He also began steering conversations away from tension. When colleagues debated routing changes or his wife pressed him about missed dinner appointments, he would nod, change the subject, or retreat to the garage. It was easier to let decisions pass him by than to risk the friction that might unravel the fragile calm he had built. At seventy-two, Tien still advised logistics for the aid network, though his role had narrowed to the safety of an air-conditioned office. The avoidance had quietly rewired his days. He delegated site visits to younger coordinators, missing the field briefings where decisions were made, and he had stopped accompanying his wife to the community center where they had volunteered for twenty years. The distance between them was not a rupture, but a slow drifting, maintained by his steady refusal to engage when voices rose or plans changed without his full consent. What finally brought him to the clinic was a Tuesday morning when a dropped file folder triggered a full-body flinch that left him gasping in the supply closet, followed by three days where the familiar images and sounds felt closer than the furniture around him. He sat across from a new counselor with his hands folded tightly in his lap, hoping to learn how to quiet the automatic inventory of danger that had grown so loud it was drowning out the present. He was most afraid that the camp would never truly be over, that he would spend the rest of his life watching exits instead of watching his wife, but he left that session with a fragile, reluctant hope that he might finally lay down the ledger he had been carrying alone for too long.
